_note: Geolocated primary sources. Files are web derivatives of the HQ archive assembled for Unit 1. 'certainty' is deliberately exposed to students: located = the record names the place; approximate = place inferred from the record; symbolic = the object has no single place and is pinned where it belongs in the argument.

sources.title: Saccharum officinarum (sugar cane)
sources.creator: Robert Bentley and Henry Trimen, Medicinal Plants
sources.place: Pinned to the New Guinea highlands — where cane was first cultivated
sources.caption: The plant at the centre of the whole story, drawn as a medicine. For most of recorded history sugar was classed as a drug, not a food.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Title: the plate comes from a book called *Medicinal Plants*. What does that title tell you about how sugar was understood in 1880, and how is that different from how you understand it?

sources.title: Two boys eating sugar cane
sources.creator: Stereograph, publisher unidentified
sources.place: Caribbean — the record does not name the island. Pinned near St Kitts because it sits with the 1901 St Kitts views.
sources.caption: The book pairs this with a 2005 photograph from the Dominican Republic and makes one point: for these children cane is food, not a treat.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Conclusion: the authors say these boys 'very likely also work in cane fields.' What in the photograph supports that inference, and what does the photograph *not* tell you?

sources.title: The Elephant Plough, Used on a Sugar Plantation in India
sources.creator: Wood engraving, Gleason's Pictorial Drawing-Room Companion, Boston
sources.place: Northern India — the engraving names no town; pinned to the Bihar cane belt
sources.caption: A British plough (Ransomes and May, of Ipswich) drawn by an Indian elephant, printed for American readers. The book asks flatly whether elephants really pulled ploughs this way or a visiting artist imagined it.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Interrelationships: an English plough, an Indian elephant, a Boston magazine. Who made this image, who was it made for, and how might that shape what it shows?
sources.correction: Often captioned 'Elephants Plowing a Cane Field' and credited to the Illustrated London News. Both are wrong: the caption above is the engraving's own, and it ran in Gleason's Pictorial.

sources.title: Buzurgmihr masters the game of chess
sources.creator: First Small Shahnama, Persian
sources.place: Pinned to Jundi Shapur (Gundeshapur), Khuzestan, Iran
sources.caption: An Indian envoy brings chess to the Persian court. The book uses this scene for the kind of India-to-Persia exchange that ran through Jundi Shapur — where scholars first wrote sugar down as a medicine, sharkara.
sources.rights: Public domain. The Metropolitan Museum of Art, 34.24.1.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Connections: name three things that travelled the same road as sugar in this period. What does it mean that ideas and crops moved together?
sources.correction: SUBSTITUTE. The book reproduces British Library Or. 1403, f. 419v — a Shahnama made in India in 1437. No free copy of that folio exists; this is the same episode in a different, earlier manuscript. The Indian origin of the book's version is part of its point, so note the difference.

sources.title: Arithmetica: Pythagoras and Boethius
sources.creator: Gregor Reisch, Margarita Philosophica
sources.place: Printed in the Upper Rhine — pinned to Strasbourg
sources.caption: Counting boards on the right, Arabic numerals on the left. Europe learned the zero from India by way of the Muslim world — the same route that carried sugar.
sources.rights: Public domain. Library of Congress copy.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Parts: who is winning, and how does the artist show it? What is the muse in the middle doing?
sources.correction: The book dates this 1501; the edition is 1503.

sources.title: The whole sugar cycle at a glance
sources.creator: Engraving, artist unidentified
sources.place: No single estate — pinned to Pernambuco, Brazil
sources.caption: Harvest, bundling, carting, grinding, boiling, cooling — every stage of the sugar machine compressed into one picture. The book warns: no real mill ever looked like this.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Conclusion: the image shows every stage happening at once. Why would an engraver do that, and what does the compression hide about how the work actually felt?

sources.title: Map of Pernambuco with a sugar mill
sources.creator: Dutch cartographer, Pernambuco under Dutch rule
sources.caption: By 1640 Pernambuco's plantations shipped some 24,000 pounds of sugar to Amsterdam alone. When Portugal took the region back, Dutch planters carried the knowledge to the Caribbean — and some Dutch Jews to New York.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Aura: the mapmaker put ships, a mill, and calm water on the same sheet. What impression is the map selling, and to whom? Whose labour is missing from it?

sources.title: Planting the sugar cane (Plate III)
sources.creator: William Clark, Ten Views in the Island of Antigua
sources.caption: Each cutting needed a hole five inches deep and five feet square. On one French island overseers beat workers who did not cut twenty-eight holes an hour.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Parts: find the overseer. How has Clark positioned him relative to everyone else, and what does that arrangement argue?

sources.title: Digging the cane holes (Plate II)
sources.creator: William Clark, Ten Views in the Island of Antigua
sources.caption: The first and heaviest task of the year, done in gangs under a driver.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Overview: Clark painted these views for people in Britain who owned Antiguan estates but had never seen one. What did they want to be shown?

sources.title: Cutting the sugar cane (Plate IV)
sources.creator: William Clark, Ten Views in the Island of Antigua
sources.caption: A man slashing, a woman binding every twelve stalks. One 1689 report expected each pair to cut and bind 4,200 stalks a day.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Interrelationships: children appear in the harvest scenes. Connect that to the book's line that everyone worked the harvest.

sources.title: The mill yard (Plate V)
sources.creator: William Clark, Ten Views in the Island of Antigua
sources.caption: The mill sat beside the field because cut cane had to reach the boiling vat within a day or two, or the crop was lost.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Pattern: why must the mill be next to the field? What does that single constraint do to the way the whole island is organised?

sources.title: The windmill and grinding house
sources.creator: After William Clark
sources.caption: The mills ran from four in the afternoon to ten the next morning, stopping only in the midday heat.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Parts: count the sources of power in this image. Which of them can be made to work eighteen hours a day?

sources.title: Sugar Mill at Work
sources.creator: Wood engraving, Ballou's Pictorial, Boston, 10 February 1855
sources.place: Generic West Indian mill — pinned to Antigua alongside the Clark plates
sources.caption: An axe or sword propped by the rollers. If a worker's hand was caught, cutting off her own arm was the only way to avoid being pulled through. Visitors remarked on how many one-armed people they saw.
sources.rights: Public domain. Boston Public Library scan via Internet Archive.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Conclusion: the blade is drawn as ordinary equipment. What does it mean that a safety tool and a mutilation tool are the same object?

sources.title: The boiling house (Plate VI)
sources.creator: William Clark, Ten Views in the Island of Antigua
sources.caption: A visitor to Brazil in 1630: 'whoever sees all the confused and noisy machinery … will say that this indeed is the image of Hell.'
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Title: Clark called this simply 'the boiling house.' Compare his title with the 1630 description. Which one is the interpretation?

sources.title: The boiling house, second view (Plate VII)
sources.creator: William Clark, Ten Views in the Island of Antigua
sources.caption: The 'boiler' — an enslaved specialist — judged the exact moment to strike, when syrup would crystallise. The book calls him part chemist, part magician.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Interrelationships: the book says special knowledge 'did not make a slave any less a slave.' What did skill buy, and what did it not buy?

sources.title: The curing house and stills (Plate VIII)
sources.creator: William Clark, Ten Views in the Island of Antigua
sources.caption: Crystals were left to dry and separate — in Brazil, tended for a month by enslaved women known as the 'mothers of the platform.'
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Parts: who is doing the skilled sorting here, and how does Clark show their expertise — or fail to?

sources.title: The distillery (Plate IX)
sources.creator: William Clark, Ten Views in the Island of Antigua
sources.caption: Molasses drained off the sugar became rum — which ships carried to Africa to buy people.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Connections: trace the rum in this building to a person on the coast of Africa. How many steps does it take?

sources.title: Sugar hogsheads (Plate X)
sources.creator: William Clark, Ten Views in the Island of Antigua
sources.caption: Packed into barrels for the eager customers the book keeps returning to — people in Britain stirring it into tea.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Conclusion: this is the moment sugar stops being labour and becomes cargo. What gets forgotten at this point in the chain?

sources.title: Shipping the sugar
sources.creator: After William Clark
sources.caption: The last West Indian scene before the Atlantic crossing.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Spatial–temporal: this is the hinge between two maps in this project. Which layer does the story move to next?

sources.title: Vacuum Pan — patent drawing, Sheet 1 of 6
sources.creator: Norbert Rillieux; US Patent No. 3,237
sources.place: New Orleans, Louisiana — the patent names him as 'of New Orleans'
sources.caption: Put this beside Clark's boiling house from 1823. There, a line of open cauldrons and a team of people ladling scalding syrup between them. Here, sealed pans that pass the heat along themselves. The drawing is what replaced those plates.
sources.rights: Public domain. National Archives and Records Administration, NAID 70663975.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Interrelationships: hold this next to Clark's boiling-house plates ([15a], [15b]). Name three things the machine removes from that room. Then ask who those three things were, and what happened to them.

sources.title: Rillieux's patent model, with the Patent Office tag
sources.creator: Norbert Rillieux
sources.place: Made for the Patent Office in Washington; pinned to New Orleans, where he worked
sources.caption: The object he actually mailed to Washington — tin, wood, and a red cloth ribbon, thirteen inches tall. The tag in the clerk's handwriting says N. Rillieux, Sugar Works. The Patent Office wrote his name down; the printed patent then assigned the invention to two engineers in Philadelphia.
sources.rights: CC0. Anacostia Community Museum, Smithsonian Institution, 1994.0001.0001.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Perspective: the model, the tag and the printed patent were made by three different hands. Whose name is on each, and who ends up owning the machine?

sources.title: The History of a Pound of Sugar
sources.creator: Children's book, published in England
sources.place: Published in London; depicts the West Indies
sources.caption: A book for British children that walks the same stages Clark painted — preparing, planting, harvesting, refining, and finally selling sweets.
sources.rights: Public domain. Baldwin Library, University of Florida.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Title: this was aimed at children in 1861 — after Britain abolished slavery. What does it choose to tell them, and what does it leave out?

sources.title: The sugar mill, from The History of a Pound of Sugar
sources.creator: Children's book, published in England
sources.caption: Verse and picture together. The book notes that even aimed at young readers, it makes the toil clear.
sources.rights: Public domain. Baldwin Library, University of Florida.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Interrelationships: read the verse against the picture. Do they agree?

sources.title: "Two pretty girls I met in a cane field," St. Kitts, B.W.I.
sources.creator: Stereograph
sources.caption: Sixty-three years after emancipation, in the same fields.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Title: the book captions this 'Two Sugar Workers.' The archive's own title is the one above. Which title is doing more work, and on whose behalf?
sources.correction: The Library of Congress title differs from the book's caption. Both are given here on purpose.

sources.title: Burning the cane field before harvest
sources.creator: Jack Delano, Farm Security Administration
sources.caption: Delano was working with the anthropologist Sidney Mintz, whose Sweetness and Power shaped this whole book.
sources.rights: Public domain. Library of Congress, FSA/OWI.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Overview: this is a government photographer in 1942, not a plantation artist in 1823. What changes in what you are shown, and what does not?

sources.title: Cutting sugar cane near Ponce, Puerto Rico
sources.creator: Edwin Rosskam, Farm Security Administration
sources.caption: The machete and the stance are the same ones in Clark's Antigua plates from 115 years earlier.
sources.rights: Public domain. Library of Congress, FSA/OWI.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Interrelationships: put this beside Clark's Plate IV. List what has changed and what has not. Which list is longer?

sources.title: Playing the cuatro at a holiday party
sources.creator: Jack Delano, Farm Security Administration
sources.caption: The book's argument about music: bomba in Puerto Rico, Maculelê in Brazil, jazz in Louisiana. When people were forbidden to speak, they played.
sources.rights: Public domain. Library of Congress, FSA/OWI.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Conclusion: the authors call music a way of saying 'we are not just bodies born to work and die.' How can a photograph of a party be evidence for a historical argument?

sources.title: Loading cane on carts, Hawaii
sources.creator: Photographer unidentified
sources.place: Hawaii — island not specified; pinned to Oahu
sources.caption: By now the workers were most often Chinese, Japanese, Filipino, Korean and Portuguese — recruited group after group to keep wages down.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Region: why did planters keep changing which country their workers came from? What did that strategy accidentally produce in Hawaii?

sources.title: Sugarcane cutter and waterboy near New Iberia, Louisiana
sources.creator: Russell Lee, Farm Security Administration
sources.caption: The state enslaved people called 'Lousy Anna' — the one American slave state where the enslaved population fell rather than grew.
sources.rights: Public domain. Library of Congress, FSA/OWI.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Parts: note the ages of the two people. Connect that to Ephraim Knowlton's 'suckling gang' and the water carriers aged eleven to fifteen.

sources.title: Stick fighting
sources.creator: Agostino Brunias
sources.caption: A contest, and a way enslaved people could show strength to each other without directly challenging a master.
sources.rights: CC0. Yale Center for British Art.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Conclusion: Brunias painted for planters. Does that make this useless as evidence of what enslaved people did — or does it make it useful in a different way?

sources.title: A maroon fighter
sources.creator: William Blake, after John Gabriel Stedman
sources.caption: Stedman came to Surinam in 1772 to fight escaped slaves, then commissioned artists to illustrate what he had seen.
sources.rights: Public domain. University of Amsterdam Library.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Overview: the man who ordered this image was fighting the man in it. How does the picture treat him, and does that surprise you?

sources.title: Trelawny Town, a maroon village
sources.creator: Engraving after a contemporary view
sources.caption: Britain signed a peace treaty with the maroons in 1739–40. Sixty years later, with Haiti in revolt nearby, it broke its word, captured as many as it could and deported them to Nova Scotia.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Region: find Cockpit Country on the map and look at the terrain. Why here? What does the landscape have to do with freedom?

sources.title: Cardiff Hall, St Ann's
sources.creator: James Hakewill, A Picturesque Tour in the Island of Jamaica
sources.caption: Built on a hill for the breeze, so the planter could look over his estate — and mostly left empty, because planters moved to England as soon as they could afford to.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Aura: Hakewill is selling a landscape. Describe the mood, then list what an accurate map of this estate would have to add.

sources.title: A view of the spring-head of Roaring River, on the estate of William Beckford Esqr.
sources.creator: George Robertson, engraved by James Mason
sources.place: Roaring River estate, near Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland, Jamaica
sources.caption: One of the twenty-four Jamaican plantations behind the fortune of the man who became Lord Mayor of London.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Interrelationships: the book says the artist wanted it 'to look peaceful and beautiful, and to make slaves look meek and humble.' Find the choices that do that work — scale, placement, posture, light.

sources.title: William Beckford, Lord Mayor of London
sources.creator: Print, London
sources.caption: 'Alderman Sugar-Cane.' He lived in England, owned two thousand people in Jamaica, and sat in Parliament — which is exactly what made American colonists furious about the sugar tax.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Connections: draw the line from Roaring River, Jamaica to a vote in the Parliament at Westminster. Who is on each end of it?

sources.title: Banquet given by Pope Clement IX for Queen Christina of Sweden
sources.creator: Pierre Paul Sevin, watercolour
sources.caption: The entire table is sculpture made of sugar. At a 1565 royal wedding in Brussels, some three thousand carved sugar pieces showed a princess's voyage, down to sugar birds in sugar cages.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Conclusion: this is food made to be looked at, not eaten. What is actually being displayed here?

sources.title: A Family of Three at Tea
sources.creator: Richard Collins
sources.caption: Sugar dish, tea canister, sugar tongs. Tea was bitter; sugar made it drinkable; and the two together turned a Caribbean crop into an English daily necessity.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Parts: list every object on the table that had to cross an ocean. Now list where each one came from.

sources.title: Silver sugar nippers
sources.creator: English silversmith
sources.caption: Sugar came as a hard loaf; you cut a serving off it. A tool this fine exists because sugar had become a thing to display.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Title: 'nippers' is a household word for a household object. What does the ordinariness of the name tell you about how far sugar had travelled since Henry III paid the equivalent of $450 for three pounds?

sources.title: Mrs Beeton's Book of Household Management, title page
sources.creator: Isabella Beeton
sources.caption: The standard manual for English households — by which point a proper home was expected to serve tea with sugar several times a day.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Overview: a book about running a house. Why is it evidence in a history of slavery?
sources.correction: The book credits a tea-service plate from Beeton 1861. No such colour plate exists — every colour plate in the digitised Beeton is from the 1923 edition. This is the genuine 1861 colour title page instead.

sources.title: Tea sold on the streets of London
sources.creator: George Cruikshank, illustration to Charles Dickens
sources.caption: In the early 1700s the average English person ate four pounds of sugar a year. A century later, eighteen. By 1900, ninety.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Interrelationships: who is buying, and where are they standing? Connect this street scene to the factory whistle on the next pin.

sources.title: A Pair of Spinning Mules
sources.creator: Engraving, England
sources.caption: Machines set the pace and workers could not choose when to stop. The break needed a cheap jolt of energy: sweet tea and a biscuit. The book's claim is blunt — English factories were built, run, and paid for by sugar.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Comparisons: compare this factory floor with Clark's boiling house. The book argues the plantation came first and taught the factory. What in the two images supports that, and what complicates it?

sources.title: Instruments used to punish and torture enslaved people
sources.creator: Illustration from Olaudah Equiano's autobiography
sources.place: Published in London; the objects were used in the West Indies
sources.caption: Clarkson brandished whips and handcuffs when he lectured. Equiano put them on the page. The abolitionists' method was to make the invisible visible to the people who benefited from it.
sources.rights: Public domain. Library of Congress / British Library.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Conclusion: why show the tools rather than the suffering? Think about what an eighteenth-century reader could be persuaded by.

sources.title: Sir John Gladstone, 1st Baronet
sources.creator: Thomas Gladstones
sources.place: Pinned to Liverpool, where he ran the firm and chaired the West India Association; his plantations were in Demerara and Jamaica
sources.caption: He owned Success, the Demerara plantation where the 1823 rebellion began. When slavery ended he was paid £106,769 for 2,508 people — the largest single award any Briton received. Then he wrote to Calcutta for replacements. One man carries the whole turn from slavery to indenture.
sources.rights: Painting public domain (artist died 1832). Reproduction: National Portrait Gallery, London, NPG 5042 — the NPG asserts copyright in the photograph. See SOURCE.md.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Connections: you drew a line from Roaring River to Westminster for Beckford. Draw Gladstone's, and make it longer — Success plantation in Demerara, this counting house in Liverpool, and a shipping office in Calcutta. What is different about the third stop?

sources.title: The Black Man's Lament; or, How to Make Sugar
sources.creator: Amelia Opie
sources.caption: A children's book whose subtitle is the whole argument: this is how to make sugar.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Title: compare this title with 'The History of a Pound of Sugar' from 1861. Both are for children. What is each one for?

sources.title: Anti-slavery reticule, Female Society of Birmingham
sources.creator: Female Society of Birmingham
sources.caption: Women met in sewing circles to make bags carrying abolitionist images — designed to shame everyone who passed into thinking about the price of the sugar in their tea.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Interrelationships: this is a handbag. Explain how a handbag becomes a political instrument, and who could use this one when they could not vote.

sources.title: A second anti-slavery reticule
sources.creator: Female Society of Birmingham
sources.caption: The Birmingham women read Elizabeth Heyrick, who argued against gradual abolition: every enslaved person must be freed at once.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Parts: what image is on the bag, and what posture is the enslaved figure in? Compare with the 1807 medal in Sierra Leone.
sources.correction: The unit lists [40] and [41] as a 'reticule' and a 'workbag.' They are two reticules by the same society; no separate workbag exists in the V&A.

sources.title: Abolition medal — obverse
sources.creator: Struck for use in Sierra Leone
sources.caption: In England, even abolitionists pictured enslaved people kneeling and pleading. On this coin, made for a colony of freed people in Africa, the two figures stand nearly equal.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Conclusion: same movement, two audiences, two images. What changes when the audience changes?

sources.title: Abolition medal — reverse
sources.creator: Struck for use in Sierra Leone
sources.caption: At noon on 25 March 1807, George III signed the law ending British involvement in the slave trade. No enslaved person was freed by it.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Spatial–temporal: 1807 ends the trade; 1833 ends slavery in the British empire; 1838 frees people. Why the gaps?

sources.title: Toussaint Louverture accepts the constitution, 7 July 1801
sources.creator: Print
sources.caption: The constitution gave him control of the whole island of Hispaniola. He called himself L'Ouverture — the opening.
sources.prompt: OPTIC — Overview: how is Toussaint dressed and posed? What is the image claiming about who he is?

sources.title: The sugar harvest in Louisiana
sources.creator: After Alfred R. Waud, engraving
sources.place: Sugar country along the Mississippi, Louisiana
sources.caption: The factory sits next to the field. Because sugar came to Louisiana late, it married the pace of the steam engine to the endless cane cycle.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Pattern: this is ten years after emancipation. What in the image has changed since slavery, and what has the machine changed instead?

sources.title: Levni — sugar and candy garden sculptures (NOT OBTAINED)
sources.creator: Levni, Surname-i Vehbi
sources.caption: For the circumcision festival of Sultan Ahmed III's son, Levni painted garden sculptures made entirely of sugar — so heavy it took eighteen men to carry each one.
sources.rights: Not openly digitised. Topkapı A.3593, fols. 161a–162b.
sources.prompt: There is no free image of this. Ask yourself: whose history gets digitised, and whose does not? That is a source question too.

sources.title: Testard — Collecting Aloe Wood (NOT OBTAINED)
sources.creator: Robinet Testard
sources.place: Pinned to the Nile — where medieval Europeans believed spices floated from Eden
sources.caption: Jean de Joinville, who had actually lived in the Muslim world, still believed people netted ginger, rhubarb and cinnamon out of a river running from the Garden of Eden.
sources.rights: Not openly digitised. Russian National Library, fr. F.v.VI,1, f. 143.
sources.prompt: SCRAP — Aura: Europeans put the source of spices in paradise. What does a wrong map tell you about the people who drew it?
